subject: Science
title: Carbon and its Compounds
summary: The chapter explains why carbon forms so many compounds (covalent bonding, tetravalency, catenation), how to name and classify them (saturated and unsaturated chains, rings, functional groups, homologous series), the four reactions every carbon compound can undergo, the chemistry of ethanol and ethanoic acid, and how soaps and detergents clean. It is the only organic chemistry a Class 10 student meets, and the board asks from it every year in every question type.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 10 Science is one 80-mark paper covering physics, chemistry and biology. This chapter belongs to Unit I, Chemical Substances: Nature and Behaviour (Chapters 1 to 4), which carries 25 marks in total. Carbon and its Compounds alone typically carries 5 to 7 marks, spread over a 1-mark MCQ or Assertion-Reason item, one 2- or 3-mark question, and very often a 5-mark question with an internal choice.

question_types.note: Counting bonds in a molecule (ethane, butane, benzene, cyclohexane), picking the odd one out of a homologous series, which hydrocarbon shows addition, the functional group of a named compound, the structure of cyclohexane, the correct statement about micelles.

Why carbon shares electrons instead of forming C<sup>4+</sup> or C<sup>4−</sup>, catenation and the strength of the C–C bond, esterification versus saponification, glacial acetic acid, propanal and propanone as isomers.

Define homologous series with an example, write the next member, name a compound by IUPAC rules, give a test to distinguish two compounds (alcohol vs acid, saturated vs unsaturated, soap vs detergent), draw an electron dot structure, or explain why covalent compounds have low melting points and do not conduct.

Reactions of ethanol or ethanoic acid with equations, structural isomers of butane or pentane, why ethanol to ethanoic acid is oxidation, addition versus substitution reaction, the role of concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, hydrogenation and its industrial use.

Almost every year: the compound identification chain (X of formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O oxidises to Y, dehydrates to Z, esterifies with Y), or a five-part question mixing definitions (homologous series, catenation), equations (combustion, oxidation, hydrogenation, esterification, saponification) and the cleaning action of soap with micelle diagram.
A passage on soaps and hard water, on hydrogenation of oils, on ethanol and its reactions, or on a homologous series, followed by four sub-parts, one of which usually carries an internal choice.

hot_topics: Compound identification chain: ethanol → ethanoic acid → ethene → ethyl ethanoate, with every equation
Cleaning action of soap: micelle formation, scum in hard water, why detergents work in hard water
Homologous series: definition, characteristics, general formulae, naming the next member
Structural isomers of butane and pentane; counting bonds in ethane, butane, benzene, cyclohexane
Why carbon forms covalent bonds and why it forms so many compounds (tetravalency, catenation)
Esterification and saponification: reactants, conditions, products, role of conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
Chemical tests: bromine water for unsaturation, sodium carbonate for a carboxylic acid, sodium metal for an alcohol
Addition versus substitution; hydrogenation of vegetable oils with a nickel catalyst
Electron dot structures of CH<sub>4</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub>, ethanoic acid, ethene, ethyne, N<sub>2</sub>, O<sub>2</sub>

sections.heading: 4.1 Bonding in Carbon – The Covalent Bond
sections.body:
Start with what carbon is. Its atomic number is 6, so its electronic configuration is 2, 4. It has four electrons in the outermost shell and needs four more to reach the stable configuration of neon (2, 8). There are three ways to reach a full shell: lose electrons, gain electrons, or share them. Carbon cannot lose four electrons to form C4+, because holding six protons with only two remaining electrons would need an enormous amount of energy. It cannot gain four electrons to form C4− either, because six protons cannot hold ten electrons. So carbon shares. It shares its four valence electrons with other atoms of carbon or with other elements, and each shared pair is a covalent bond. This argument, in these three steps, is a 2- or 3-mark question and an Assertion-Reason favourite.

NCERT builds covalent bonding from the simplest cases. Two hydrogen atoms (1 electron each) share one pair to form H2: a single bond, and each hydrogen now has the helium configuration. Two oxygen atoms (2, 6) each need two electrons, so they share two pairs: a double bond, O=O. Two nitrogen atoms (2, 5) share three pairs: a triple bond, N≡N. In methane, CH4, the carbon atom shares one electron with each of four hydrogen atoms, forming four single C–H bonds. In water, oxygen shares one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms and keeps two lone pairs.

Covalent compounds have a recognisable set of physical properties, and the board keeps asking for the reason behind each. They have low melting and boiling points because the molecules are held together by weak intermolecular forces, even though the bonds inside each molecule are strong. They are generally poor conductors of electricity because bonding does not produce ions; there are no charged particles to carry the current. Many are gases or volatile liquids at room temperature. Contrast this with ionic compounds, which are solids with high melting points and conduct when molten or dissolved.

Two more points the examiner rewards. Carbon forms strong bonds with itself and with other elements because its atom is small, so the shared electrons are held close to both nuclei. And the older textbook's box on allotropes (diamond, graphite, fullerenes) is not in the rationalised chapter, so a one-line mention is enough: diamond has each carbon bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional lattice, graphite has layers of hexagonal rings and conducts electricity.

formulas.expr: Carbon: Z = 6, configuration 2, 4; valency 4
where: number of covalent bonds carbon forms to reach the neon configuration

formulas.expr: Single bond H–H, double bond O=O, triple bond N≡N

sections.tip: In an electron dot structure, show every valence electron of every atom, keep the shared pairs between the two symbols, and do not forget the lone pairs on O, N, S and Cl. A dot structure of H<sub>2</sub>O without the two lone pairs on oxygen loses a mark.

sections.heading: 4.2 Versatile Nature of Carbon
sections.body:
Carbon forms more compounds than all the other elements put together: millions are known, and the number keeps growing. NCERT gives two reasons, and every board answer to 'why does carbon form so many compounds' must name both.

The first is catenation: carbon atoms can bond to other carbon atoms to give long chains, branched chains and rings. The chains can be very long, and the carbon–carbon bonds can be single, double or triple. No other element does this to the same extent. Silicon, just below carbon in the same group, forms hydrogen compounds with chains of only seven or eight silicon atoms, and those compounds are very reactive. The difference is bond strength: the C–C bond is strong, so carbon chains are stable, while the Si–Si bond is weak.

The second is tetravalency. Carbon has a valency of four, so each carbon atom can bond with four other atoms. Those atoms can be carbon or a different element such as oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and so on. Changing the element attached changes the properties of the compound, which multiplies the possibilities enormously.

Why are these bonds strong? Carbon is a small atom, so the shared electron pairs sit close to the nucleus and are held tightly. Elements with larger atoms form much weaker bonds. This is why compounds of carbon are stable in the way that compounds of silicon are not.

Hydrocarbons are compounds of carbon and hydrogen only, and they are where the chapter starts counting. The simplest is methane, CH4. Then comes ethane, C2H6, where two carbons are joined by a single bond and the remaining six valencies are taken by hydrogen. In an exam you should be able to draw any hydrocarbon in three ways: link the carbon skeleton first, then add hydrogens until every carbon has four bonds, then, if asked, convert it to an electron dot structure by replacing each bond with a shared pair of dots. A frequent 1-mark question asks how many covalent bonds ethane has: six C–H and one C–C, so seven.

formulas.expr: Ethane C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>: 6 C–H + 1 C–C = 7 covalent bonds
Butane C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>: 10 C–H + 3 C–C = 13 covalent bonds
where: a chain of n carbons has n − 1 C–C single bonds

sections.tip: If the question says 'why does carbon form a large number of compounds', write both catenation and tetravalency and add one sentence on the strong C–C bond due to carbon's small size. Two words alone do not earn full marks.

sections.heading: 4.2.1 Saturated and Unsaturated Carbon Compounds
sections.body:
Take ethane, C2H6, and ask what happens if we remove one hydrogen from each carbon. The two carbons then have one unused valency each. They satisfy those valencies by sharing a second pair of electrons between themselves, giving a double bond, C=C. That compound is ethene, C2H4. Remove one more hydrogen from each carbon and the carbons share a third pair: a triple bond, C≡C, in ethyne, C2H2.

This gives the classification the whole chapter uses. Compounds of carbon that contain only single bonds between carbon atoms are saturated: every carbon is bonded to the maximum number of other atoms it can hold. Compounds with one or more double or triple bonds between carbon atoms are unsaturated. Saturated hydrocarbons are alkanes, with the general formula CnH2n+2. Hydrocarbons with a double bond are alkenes, CnH2n, and with a triple bond are alkynes, CnH2n−2. Notice that there is no alkene or alkyne with one carbon; the first alkene is ethene and the first alkyne is ethyne.

Unsaturated compounds are more reactive than saturated ones, because the extra shared pair in a double or triple bond is available for reaction: it opens up and lets other atoms add on. That single sentence is the reason behind addition reactions, the bromine water test and hydrogenation, all of which come later.

Exams test this section through formulae. Given a molecular formula, decide which series it belongs to: C3H8 fits CnH2n+2, so it is an alkane, saturated, and will not show addition. C4H8 fits CnH2n, so it is an alkene and will show addition. C3H4 fits CnH2n−2, so it is propyne with one triple bond. The 'odd one out' MCQ works the same way: among C5H12, C6H14, C7H14 and C8H18, only C7H14 fails the alkane formula, so it belongs to a different series.

formulas.expr: Alkanes C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>, alkenes C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>, alkynes C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−2</sub>
where: number of carbon atoms (n ≥ 1 for alkanes, n ≥ 2 for alkenes and alkynes)

sections.tip: A quick check for 'saturated or not': count hydrogens. If H = 2C + 2 the compound is a saturated open chain. Fewer hydrogens means a double bond, a triple bond or a ring.

sections.heading: 4.2.2 Chains, Branches and Rings
sections.body:
Carbon skeletons need not be straight. NCERT introduces branching with butane, C4H10. You can arrange four carbons as a straight chain, CH3–CH2–CH2–CH3, or as a three-carbon chain with the fourth carbon attached to the middle one, CH3–CH(CH3)–CH3. Both have the formula C4H10, but they are different compounds with different properties. Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are called structural isomers. Methane, ethane and propane have no isomers because there is only one way to join one, two or three carbons; isomerism begins at butane. Pentane, C5H12, has three structural isomers: the straight chain, a four-carbon chain with one methyl branch on the second carbon, and a three-carbon chain with two methyl branches on the middle carbon.

Carbon also forms rings. Cyclohexane, C6H12, is a ring of six carbons joined by single bonds, each carbon carrying two hydrogens. It is saturated even though it has fewer hydrogens than hexane, C6H14, because the ring uses up two valencies. Cyclopentane, C5H10, is a ring of five carbons and has 15 single bonds in all (5 C–C and 10 C–H). Benzene, C6H6, is a six-membered ring with alternate single and double bonds: 3 C=C double bonds, 3 C–C single bonds and 6 C–H bonds, so 9 single bonds and 3 double bonds in total. Benzene is an unsaturated cyclic hydrocarbon; cyclohexane is a saturated one.

Counting is the main exam skill here. For any open-chain alkane of n carbons there are n − 1 C–C bonds and 2n + 2 C–H bonds; for a saturated ring of n carbons there are n C–C bonds and 2n C–H bonds. Cyclohexane therefore has 6 + 12 = 18 single bonds. Draw rings as regular polygons with a carbon at each corner and be explicit about the hydrogens if the question says 'structure' rather than 'skeleton'.

Whenever you draw an isomer, check that every carbon has exactly four bonds and that the molecular formula still adds up. Most lost marks in isomer questions come from a carbon with five bonds or a hydrogen count that has drifted.

formulas.expr: Open-chain alkane C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>: (n − 1) C–C bonds and (2n + 2) C–H bonds
Saturated ring C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>: n C–C bonds and 2n C–H bonds
Benzene C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>: 3 C=C, 3 C–C, 6 C–H

sections.tip: Two drawings that look different but are really the same chain bent differently are NOT isomers. Before you claim an isomer, name the longest chain and see if the branch position genuinely differs.

sections.heading: 4.2.3 Will you be my Friend? Heteroatoms and Functional Groups
sections.body:
In a hydrocarbon, one or more hydrogen atoms can be replaced by other atoms or groups of atoms in a way that keeps the valency of carbon satisfied. The element that replaces hydrogen is called a heteroatom: oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine, bromine and so on. The heteroatom, or the group containing it, gives the compound its characteristic properties regardless of the length of the carbon chain. Such a group is called a functional group. The name says it well: the functional group is where the chemistry happens.

The functional groups in NCERT, with the way they are written in a structure, are: halogen (–Cl, –Br, called halo group), alcohol (–OH), aldehyde (–CHO, a carbon double bonded to oxygen and single bonded to hydrogen, always at the end of a chain), ketone (a carbon double bonded to oxygen with carbon atoms on both sides, so never at the end of a chain), and carboxylic acid (–COOH, a carbon carrying both a double bonded oxygen and an –OH). Alkenes and alkynes are also treated as having a functional group: the C=C double bond and the C≡C triple bond.

Two consequences are tested. First, the aldehyde group cannot be in the middle of a chain because its carbon has already used three valencies (two on oxygen, one on hydrogen), leaving only one for the chain. Second, a ketone needs at least three carbons, so the first ketone is propanone, CH3COCH3. Propanal, CH3CH2CHO, and propanone are both C3H6O; they have the same molecular formula but different functional groups, so they are structural isomers. This pair was an Assertion-Reason item in 2025.

Learn to spot the group from a written formula. CH3CHO is an aldehyde. C2H5COOH is a carboxylic acid. CH3COCH2CH3 is a ketone (butanone). CH3CH2Br carries a halo group. A compound of formula C2H6O that reacts with sodium is the alcohol, ethanol; a compound of formula C2H4O2 that fizzes with sodium carbonate is the acid, ethanoic acid. These identifications are the entry point to every 5-mark identification question.

formulas.expr: Functional groups: –Cl/–Br (halo), –OH (alcohol), –CHO (aldehyde), >C=O (ketone), –COOH (carboxylic acid), C=C (alkene), C≡C (alkyne)
where: an atom other than C or H that replaces hydrogen in a hydrocarbon

sections.tip: When asked to 'name the functional group', write the name (aldehyde) and the formula (–CHO). Writing only one of them is a half answer.

sections.heading: 4.2.4 Homologous Series
sections.body:
A homologous series is a series of carbon compounds in which the same functional group substitutes for hydrogen in a carbon chain, and successive members differ from each other by a –CH2– unit. The alkanes are the simplest example: CH4, C2H6, C3H8, C4H10. Alcohols form another: CH3OH, C2H5OH, C3H7OH, C4H9OH. So do aldehydes (HCHO, CH3CHO, C2H5CHO), carboxylic acids (HCOOH, CH3COOH, C2H5COOH), alkenes and alkynes.

The examiner expects these characteristics, and the definition question usually asks for two or three of them:

  • Successive members differ by a –CH2– unit, so their molecular masses differ by 14 u (12 for carbon plus 2 for hydrogen).
  • All members can be represented by one general formula, such as CnH2n+2 for alkanes or CnH2n+1OH for alcohols.
  • All members contain the same functional group, so their chemical properties are similar. The chemistry is decided by the functional group, not the chain length.
  • Physical properties such as melting point, boiling point and solubility change gradually along the series as molecular mass increases, because the intermolecular forces grow with size. Methane, ethane, propane and butane are gases; pentane onwards are liquids; the very long ones are waxy solids.

Two things trap students. The first is the phrase 'chemical properties show gradation'. They do not; chemical properties stay similar, and it is the physical properties that show gradation. The second is thinking that a homologous series is defined by the formula alone. C4H8 (an alkene) and C5H12 (an alkane) differ by CH4, not CH2, and have different functional groups, so they are not homologues.

Typical short questions: write the next homologue of propanol (butanol, C4H9OH); write the first two members of the series with a –Br group (bromomethane CH3Br and bromoethane C2H5Br); give the third member of the aldehyde series (propanal). Always give both the name and the formula.

formulas.expr: Successive homologues differ by –CH<sub>2</sub>–, i.e. by 14 u
where: 12 u for carbon + 2 × 1 u for hydrogen

formulas.expr: Alcohols C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+1</sub>OH; aldehydes C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O; carboxylic acids C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O<sub>2</sub>
where: number of carbon atoms including the one in the functional group

sections.tip: For the 3-mark version, write the definition, one full example series with at least three members and formulae, and then two characteristics. Marking schemes split the marks exactly this way.

sections.heading: 4.2.5 Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds
sections.body:
Naming follows a fixed two-step recipe that NCERT gives and that the board tests through 'name the following' and 'draw the structure of' questions.

Step 1. Count the carbon atoms in the longest chain and take the root word: meth (1), eth (2), prop (3), but (4), pent (5), hex (6). A saturated chain takes the suffix -ane; a double bond changes it to -ene and a triple bond to -yne. So C3H8 is propane, C3H6 is propene, C3H4 is propyne.

Step 2. Add the functional group. Halogens are added as a prefix: chloro-, bromo-. The others are added as a suffix that replaces the final -e of the hydrocarbon name: -ol for alcohol, -al for aldehyde, -one for ketone, -oic acid for carboxylic acid. Hence CH3OH is methanol, C2H5OH is ethanol, HCHO is methanal, CH3CHO is ethanal, CH3COCH3 is propanone, CH3COOH is ethanoic acid, CH3CH2Cl is chloroethane, CH3Br is bromomethane.

Some names you should be able to write and draw on demand: butanone, CH3COCH2CH3, a four-carbon ketone; hexanal, CH3(CH2)4CHO, a six-carbon aldehyde; bromopentane, C5H11Br, which has structural isomers because the bromine can sit on different carbons of the chain and the chain itself can branch; propanoic acid, C2H5COOH; hex-1-yne, HC≡C–CH2–CH2–CH2–CH3. Esters are named from the alcohol part and then the acid part: the ester of ethanol and ethanoic acid is ethyl ethanoate, CH3COOC2H5.

Two reminders. The carbon of –CHO and –COOH counts in the chain: ethanoic acid has two carbons in total, not two plus one. And an aldehyde or acid group is always on carbon 1, so you never need a position number for it, whereas a ketone or a double bond in a longer chain may need one (butan-2-one, but-1-ene). At Class 10 level, the board rarely asks for positional numbers, but writing but-1-ene rather than butene is never penalised.

formulas.expr: Root: meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex (1 to 6 C) + -ane / -ene / -yne
Suffixes: -ol (alcohol), -al (aldehyde), -one (ketone), -oic acid (carboxylic acid); prefixes: chloro-, bromo-
where: replaces the final 'e' of the parent alkane name

sections.tip: Read the formula backwards if the group is on the right: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO is propanal, three carbons, and the CHO carbon is carbon 1.

sections.heading: 4.3 Chemical Properties of Carbon Compounds: 4.3.1 Combustion
sections.body:
Carbon, in all its forms, burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide along with heat and light. Most carbon compounds burn the same way, releasing a lot of heat, which is why they are used as fuels. The equations NCERT gives are: C + O2 → CO2 + heat and light; CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O + heat and light; and CH3CH2OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O + heat and light. Balance them yourself in the exam rather than relying on memory: count carbons, then hydrogens, then oxygens.

The flame tells you about the compound. Saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean blue flame in good supply of air. Unsaturated hydrocarbons burn with a yellow, sooty flame, because the higher proportion of carbon in them does not burn completely and the unburnt carbon particles glow yellow. A saturated hydrocarbon burning in a limited supply of air also gives a sooty flame, which is why the outside of a cooking vessel blackens when the burner holes are blocked and the fuel does not burn completely. This is NCERT exercise question 3 and a regular 1-mark MCQ.

Burning coal and petroleum releases sulphur and nitrogen oxides as well, which cause pollution. Coal and petroleum formed from the remains of living organisms over millions of years and are therefore called fossil fuels.

A related in-text question asks why oxygen and ethyne are burnt together for welding rather than ethyne and air. Air is mostly nitrogen, so the supply of oxygen is limited, ethyne burns incompletely with a sooty flame and the temperature is low. With pure oxygen the ethyne burns completely and releases a very high temperature, enough to melt metal.

Why are carbon compounds good fuels? They contain a lot of energy per unit mass, they burn readily in air with a clean flame, they release a great deal of heat, and the products, carbon dioxide and water, do not leave a residue. That four-point list answers NCERT exercise 9 in full.

formulas.expr: CH<sub>4</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + heat and light
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O + heat and light
where: burns with a clean blue flame, hence used as a fuel

sections.tip: Blue flame means complete combustion of a saturated compound in enough air; sooty yellow flame means either an unsaturated compound or a poor air supply. The MCQ will make you tell the two apart.

sections.heading: 4.3.2 Oxidation
sections.body:
Combustion is a complete oxidation, but carbon compounds can also be oxidised gently and selectively. NCERT's example is the conversion of an alcohol to a carboxylic acid: ethanol is converted to ethanoic acid by alkaline potassium permanganate or by acidified potassium dichromate, on heating. The equation is written with the oxidising agent above the arrow: CH3CH2OH → (alkaline KMnO4 + heat, or acidified K2Cr2O7 + heat) → CH3COOH.

Substances such as alkaline KMnO4 and acidified K2Cr2O7 that are capable of adding oxygen to other substances are called oxidising agents. That one sentence is an in-text question and a 1-mark board question.

The activity behind this is a favourite for the 3-mark 'observation' question. Take about 3 mL of ethanol in a test tube, warm it gently in a water bath, and add a 5% solution of alkaline potassium permanganate drop by drop. At first the purple colour disappears as each drop is added, because the permanganate is being used up to oxidise the ethanol. After enough has been added the colour no longer disappears, because all the ethanol has been oxidised and the excess permanganate remains. A 5% solution means 5 g of KMnO4 dissolved in 95 g of water.

Why is this an oxidation? Compare the formulae. Ethanol is C2H6O and ethanoic acid is C2H4O2. The product has gained an oxygen atom and lost two hydrogen atoms. Addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen is oxidation, so the change is an oxidation reaction. Give both the gain of oxygen and the loss of hydrogen when the question is for 2 marks.

The same reasoning extends to other alcohols: warm propanol with alkaline KMnO4 and the purple colour fades as propanoic acid forms. A question that gives you an unknown alcohol and an oxidising agent wants the corresponding acid, named with the same carbon count.

formulas.expr: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + 2[O] → (alk. KMnO<sub>4</sub> or acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, heat) → CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + H<sub>2</sub>O
where: oxygen supplied by the oxidising agent; NCERT writes the reaction without [O], with the reagent above the arrow

formulas.expr: 5% KMnO<sub>4</sub> = 5 g KMnO<sub>4</sub> in 95 g water
where: mass of solute per 100 g of solution

sections.tip: Write 'alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>' or 'acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>', with the word alkaline or acidified. Naked KMnO<sub>4</sub> with no condition is marked incomplete.

sections.heading: 4.3.3 Addition Reaction
sections.body:
Unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst such as palladium or nickel to give saturated hydrocarbons. The double or triple bond opens and each carbon takes on a hydrogen: CH2=CH2 + H2 → (Ni catalyst) → CH3–CH3. The reaction is called hydrogenation, and it is an addition reaction because two reactants combine into one product with nothing left over. A catalyst is a substance that causes a reaction to occur or proceed at a different rate without itself being affected.

The industrial application is the hydrogenation of vegetable oils. Vegetable oils generally have long unsaturated carbon chains, while animal fats have saturated chains. When a vegetable oil is heated with hydrogen in the presence of nickel, the double bonds are hydrogenated, the oil becomes solid at room temperature and the product is sold as vanaspati or hydrogenated ghee. NCERT adds the health point: oils containing unsaturated fatty acids are healthier for cooking than saturated fats, and animal fats have saturated chains that are harmful for health. This is NCERT exercise 12 and a regular case-based passage.

Addition also underlies the chemical test for unsaturation, which the board asks as 'give a test to distinguish between ethane and ethene' or 'between butter and cooking oil'. Add a few drops of bromine water to each sample and shake. The unsaturated compound (ethene, or the unsaturated cooking oil) decolourises the reddish-brown bromine water because bromine adds across the double bond. The saturated compound (ethane, or butter, which is largely saturated) does not decolourise it. Write the observation for both samples, not just the positive one.

To answer NCERT exercise 13, pick out the unsaturated formulae: C3H6 (propene) and C2H2 (ethyne) undergo addition; C2H6, C3H8 and CH4 are alkanes and do not.

formulas.expr: CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → (Ni or Pd catalyst) → CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>
where: addition of H<sub>2</sub> to an unsaturated compound
Ni or Pd; changes the rate without being consumed

formulas.expr: R–CH=CH–R + Br<sub>2</sub> (aq) → R–CHBr–CHBr–R (bromine water decolourised)
where: reddish-brown bromine water loses colour only with an unsaturated compound

sections.tip: The hydrogenation answer must contain the word catalyst and the name nickel (or palladium). The examiner looks for the catalyst specifically.

sections.heading: 4.3.4 Substitution Reaction
sections.body:
Saturated hydrocarbons are fairly unreactive. They do not react with most reagents, and they cannot show addition because there is no double or triple bond to open. But in the presence of sunlight, chlorine adds to hydrocarbons rapidly, replacing hydrogen atoms one by one. The reaction with methane is CH4 + Cl2 → (in the presence of sunlight) → CH3Cl + HCl. Because one atom (chlorine) takes the place of another (hydrogen), this is a substitution reaction. If more chlorine is available the substitution continues to give CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4; at Class 10 the first step is enough unless the question asks for the series.

Chlorine attacks higher alkanes the same way, so the reaction gives a mixture of products with the chlorine on different carbons. The condition, sunlight, is what the examiner reads first. Without it, chlorine and methane do not react at room temperature.

The 3-mark comparison question is 'distinguish between addition and substitution reactions with one example each'. Put it in a table or in two parallel sentences. Addition: shown by unsaturated compounds; the double or triple bond breaks and atoms add to both carbons; two reactants give one product; example, ethene plus hydrogen with nickel gives ethane. Substitution: shown by saturated compounds; a hydrogen atom is replaced by another atom or group; two reactants give two products; example, methane plus chlorine in sunlight gives chloromethane and hydrogen chloride. That covers all the marking points.

The substitution reaction also explains why a compound of formula C4H10 reacts with chlorine in sunlight (it is butane, an alkane) but does not decolourise bromine water. Reactions are decided by saturation, so decide first whether the compound is saturated, then choose the reaction.

formulas.expr: CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → (sunlight) → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + HCl
where: one atom replaces another; two products are formed

sections.tip: In addition reactions there is one product; in substitution there are two (the new compound plus HCl). If your equation for a substitution has one product, you have written an addition.

sections.heading: 4.4.1 Properties of Ethanol
sections.body:
Ethanol, CH3CH2OH, is a colourless liquid at room temperature, with a boiling point of 351 K (78 °C), and is commonly called alcohol. It is soluble in water in all proportions and is a good solvent, which is why it is used in medicines such as tincture of iodine, cough syrups and many tonics. In the exam, 'properties of ethanol' means two things: these physical facts and the two chemical reactions below.

Reaction with sodium. Like water, ethanol reacts with sodium metal to give hydrogen gas and sodium ethoxide: 2Na + 2CH3CH2OH → 2CH3CH2ONa + H2. Bubbles of a gas that burns with a pop sound are the evidence for hydrogen. This is the test that identifies an alcohol (and also a carboxylic acid, which reacts the same way), and it is the 'reacts with sodium to give a gas that burns with a pop' clue in identification questions.

Dehydration to ethene. Heating ethanol at 443 K with excess concentrated sulphuric acid removes a molecule of water and gives ethene: CH3CH2OH → (hot conc. H2SO4, 443 K) → CH2=CH2 + H2O. Concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a dehydrating agent here, because it removes water from ethanol. The three things marked are the temperature, the word 'excess concentrated' and the role of the acid.

NCERT also discusses the effect of alcohol on living beings. Even small amounts of dilute ethanol cause drunkenness, and drinking pure ethanol is lethal. Ethanol is also used industrially, and to prevent misuse of industrial alcohol it is made unfit for drinking by adding poisonous substances such as methanol; dyes are added to colour it blue so it is recognised. This is called denatured alcohol. Methanol is dangerous because even small quantities cause death: it is oxidised to methanal in the liver, which reacts rapidly with cell components and causes the protoplasm to coagulate; it also affects the optic nerve and causes blindness.

Ethanol is also a good fuel. Sugarcane juice can be fermented to give ethanol, and mixing it with petrol (gasohol) makes a cleaner fuel that produces only CO2 and water on burning.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH → (excess conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, 443 K) → CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

sections.tip: In dehydration the sulphuric acid is a dehydrating agent; in esterification it is a catalyst (and also absorbs water). Students swap these two roles. Attach the right role to the right reaction.

sections.heading: 4.4.2 Properties of Ethanoic Acid
sections.body:
Ethanoic acid, CH3COOH, is commonly called acetic acid and belongs to the carboxylic acid group. A 5 to 8% solution of it in water is vinegar, used as a preservative in pickles. Pure ethanoic acid melts at 290 K (17 °C), so it often freezes in cold climates in winter; that is why it is called glacial acetic acid. Carboxylic acids are weak acids: unlike mineral acids such as HCl they ionise only partly in water, so a solution of ethanoic acid has a higher pH than a solution of hydrochloric acid of the same concentration.

Esterification. Ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid as catalyst, on warming, to give the ester ethyl ethanoate and water: CH3COOH + CH3CH2OH → (acid catalyst) → CH3COOC2H5 + H2O. Esters are sweet-smelling substances used in making perfumes and as flavouring agents. The sweet smell is the observation the examiner wants in an activity question.

Saponification. On treatment with sodium hydroxide, which is a base, an ester is converted back to the alcohol and the sodium salt of the carboxylic acid: CH3COOC2H5 + NaOH → C2H5OH + CH3COONa. This reaction is called saponification because it is used to prepare soap: soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids, made by treating esters (fats and oils) with alkali.

Reaction with a base. Like a mineral acid, ethanoic acid neutralises sodium hydroxide to give a salt and water: NaOH + CH3COOH → CH3COONa + H2O. The salt is sodium ethanoate (sodium acetate).

Reaction with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates. Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate and sodium hydrogencarbonate to give the salt, carbon dioxide and water: 2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2; CH3COOH + NaHCO3 → CH3COONa + H2O + CO2. The brisk effervescence of CO2, which turns lime water milky, is the chemical test that distinguishes a carboxylic acid from an alcohol: ethanol gives no gas with sodium carbonate.

Exercise 7 asks how to differentiate ethanol and ethanoic acid. Physical: ethanoic acid has a pungent vinegar-like smell and freezes at 290 K; ethanol has a pleasant smell and boils at 351 K. Chemical: ethanoic acid turns blue litmus red and gives CO2 with NaHCO3; ethanol does neither.

sections.heading: 4.5 Soaps and Detergents
sections.body:
A soap molecule has two ends with different properties. The long hydrocarbon chain is hydrophobic: it does not dissolve in water but dissolves in oil and grease. The ionic end, –COO−Na+, is hydrophilic: it dissolves in water. Soaps are the sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids, for example sodium stearate, C17H35COONa.

Micelle formation. When soap is added to water, the molecules arrange themselves so that the hydrophobic tails are away from the water and the hydrophilic heads face the water. In the bulk of the water this produces a spherical cluster called a micelle, with the hydrocarbon tails pointing inward and the ionic heads on the outside. Micelles form in water because there is a medium that the ionic end can dissolve in while the tail cannot; in a solvent such as ethanol the hydrocarbon tail dissolves as well, so no micelle forms. That is the answer to NCERT exercise 8.

Cleaning action. Most dirt is oily and does not dissolve in water. When soap solution is applied to a dirty cloth, the hydrophobic tails of the soap molecules dissolve in the oily dirt while the ionic heads stay in the water. The soap molecules surround the oil droplet and form a micelle with the dirt trapped at the centre. The micelles stay suspended in water as a colloid; they do not come together and precipitate because the charged heads on their surfaces repel each other. Rinsing with water carries the micelles, and the dirt with them, away from the cloth. Agitation (beating the cloth or the action of a washing machine) helps to loosen the trapped dirt and remove it completely. Soap solution also scatters light, which is why it looks cloudy.

Hard water and scum. Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts. The Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions react with soap to form insoluble calcium and magnesium salts of the fatty acid, which appear as a white, sticky precipitate called scum. Soap therefore does not lather well in hard water, and a good deal of soap is wasted forming scum before any lather appears. Soap is basic in nature, so it turns red litmus blue and leaves blue litmus unchanged (exercise 11).

Detergents. Detergents are generally ammonium or sulphonate salts of long-chain carboxylic acids. Their charged end does not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions, so they remain effective in hard water. They are used in shampoos and in products for cleaning clothes. Because a detergent lathers in both hard and soft water, you cannot use it to test whether water is hard; only soap shows the difference.

Carbon has four valence electrons and forms four covalent bonds, with carbon or with other elements such as H, O, N, S and halogens.
A compound containing only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes, alkenes and alkynes are the three families.
A carbon compound in which the carbon atoms are joined only by single bonds, so each carbon holds the maximum number of atoms.
A carbon compound with at least one double or triple bond between carbon atoms. More reactive than saturated compounds; shows addition reactions.
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements of atoms, for example the two isomers of butane.
An atom other than carbon or hydrogen (O, N, S, Cl, Br) that replaces hydrogen in a hydrocarbon.
The atom or group of atoms attached to the carbon chain that decides the chemical properties of the compound, such as –OH, –CHO, –COOH.
A series of carbon compounds with the same functional group in which successive members differ by a –CH<sub>2</sub>– unit and hence by 14 u.
Burning of a compound in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water with the release of heat and light.
A substance capable of adding oxygen to another substance, such as alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> or acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>.
